In which place, dearest brother, we must consider, for the sake of the faith and the religion of the sacerdotal office which we discharge, whether the account can be satisfactory in the day of judgment for a priest of God, who maintains, and approves, and acquiesces in the baptism of blasphemers, when the Lord threatens, and says, "And now, O ye priests, this commandment is for you: if ye will not hear, and if ye will not lay it to heart to give glory unto my name, saith the Lord Almighty, I will even send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessings." Does he give glory to God, who communicates with the baptism of Marcion? Does he give glory to God, who judges that remission of sins is granted among those who blaspheme against God? Does he give glory to God, who affirms that sons are born to God without, of an adulterer and a harlot? Does he give glory to God, who does not hold the unity and truth that arise from the divine law, but maintains heresies against the Church? Does he give glory to God, who, a friend of heretics and an enemy to Christians, thinks that the priests of God, who support the truth of Christ and the unity of the Church, are to be excommunicated? If glory is thus given to God, if the fear and the discipline of God is thus preserved by His worshippers and His priests, let us cast away our arms; let us give ourselves up to captivity; let us deliver to the devil the ordination of the Gospel, the appointment of Christ, the majesty of God; let the sacraments of the divine warfare be loosed; let the standards of the heavenly camp be betrayed; and let the Church succumb and yield to heretics, light to darkness, faith to perfidy, hope to despair, reason to error, immortality to death, love to hatred, truth to falsehood, Christ to Antichrist!
Commentary on Malachi

Hence it is said in its proper sense to the priests that, if they will not hear and keep it in their heart, so as to give glory to the name of the Lord by good conduct, but on the contrary his name is cursed among the nations because of them, he will send upon them want of all good things, and turn their blessings into a curse. Those who abuse health for lust, and turn riches into luxury, and disfigure a good reputation by sordid conduct, these change the blessings of God into a curse. Or else, since the commandment is given in its proper sense to the priests, their blessings are turned into a curse when they do not bless the saints from a true affection of the heart, as Isaac blessed Jacob, and Jacob the patriarchs, and Moses the twelve tribes, but through sweet words and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent; and those who act wickedly are blessed by them, and they flatter sinners, provided they are rich, and fawn upon their vices; of whom it is said: My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray, and supplant the paths of your feet.
Commentary on Malachi

And it will take you, he says, with it, that is, the dung of your solemnities, so that your stinking faces may be befouled by the putrid admixture of dung; and so that, from the fact that I cast you away, you may understand that I am the very one who once chose your father Levi, and through Levi Aaron, and granted you the glory of the priesthood, that my covenant or testament might be with Levi, and he might minister to me in an eternal priesthood. It is to be noted that the Hebrew word brith Aquila translates συνθήκην, that is, covenant; the LXX always διαθήκην, that is, testament; and that in very many places of the Scriptures testament means not the will of the dead, but the covenant of the living.
Commentary on Malachi

And because, for what we have translated: The dung will take you with it, the Seventy translated: And I will take you up together, an interpretation is supplied: that after the priests have been covered with shame and disgrace, and have understood their sin, and have done penance, they are then taken up by the Lord; and that what follows fits this sense: And you shall know that I have sent this commandment to you. But the former interpretation seems to me the true one, lest among words of threatening he should have placed the words of one who coaxes, especially since what follows also speaks of the indignation of God.
Commentary on Malachi

Behold, I will cast the arm at you, and I will scatter upon your face the dung of your solemnities, and it will take you with it. And you shall know that I have sent to you your commandment, that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Behold, I will separate the shoulder from you, and I will scatter the stomach upon your face, the stomach of your solemnities, and I will receive you together; and you shall know that I have sent to you this commandment, that my testament might be with the Levites, says the Lord Almighty. Since he is speaking to the priests: I will cast, he says, into your faces the things you think holier in the law, and granted to you by God from the sacrificial victims as a reward for virtues. The arm, for which the LXX translated shoulder, that is, the right shoulder of the animal. And I will scatter, he says, ἔνυστρον, that is, the stomach, or according to the Hebrews, dung, that is, phares, μετωνυμικῶς (by metonymy), naming that which is contained in place of that which contains it; for the shoulder and the breast and the tongue and the stomach, and the things described in Leviticus, the priests received from the sacrificial victims. All these, he declares, he casts away for their sins and throws into the faces of the priests, so that, namely, those who offer may be such as the things that are offered.
Commentary on Malachi

Now God willed all men indeed, but especially priests, to have no blemish, and to adorn either the shoulder or the arm with good works. In the breast a good conscience is signified; in the tongue holy confession, so that what we believe with the heart unto justice we may confess with the mouth unto salvation. In the stomach too, to have nothing deadly, but what sustains and quickens our life; for unless food is digested in the stomach, and the body is watered by its juice, the body wastes away, lacks strength, and is borne toward death. But we turn everything to the contrary, so that the Lord casts the arm at us, or separates our works from the works of the saints; and we, who were commanded to anoint our head, and when fasting to wash our face from the filth of sins, and with unveiled face to contemplate the glory of the Lord, now say: The confusion of my face has covered me; and like Cain our face has fallen, nor can we fulfil what was commanded: Lift up your eyes and see, but we have faces smeared and polluted with the dung of vices, and we say: My scars have putrefied and are corrupted, from the face of my folly. Hence all these things have been turned into dung, as Scripture says: And the dung will take you with it, namely the dung with which our faces are smeared, we who ought to have come full and clean to the solemnities of God, and either to eat the flesh of the lamb with our shoes on, or, when seven weeks were completed, to offer God the fruits of our works, or to live as passers-through in the tabernacles of this world, and to say: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.
Commentary on Malachi

My covenant with him was of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he trembled before the face of my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips; in peace and in equity he walked with me, and he turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. LXX: My testament with him was of life and peace, and I gave him fear, that he might fear me and be afraid before the face of my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. In peace, directing, he walked with me, and he converted many from iniquity. For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and the law shall be sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord Almighty. The office of the perfect priest is described in the person of God: what he ought to be, and what he wished him to be who commanded that he should be. For above he had said: That my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts, and through the patriarch Levi it came down to his posterity, Aaron and Eleazar, Phinehas and the rest who were born of his stock. Now at the end he says: You have made void the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts. From this it is clear that everything said through Levi pertains to the priests, and especially to the high priest. We read in Numbers of Phinehas, who struck Zimri with the Midianite harlot with a dagger: Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has made my fury rest from the sons of Israel, because he was jealous with my zeal against them; and I did not destroy the sons of Israel in my zeal, saying thus: Behold, I will give him a testament of peace, and it shall be to him and to his seed after him a testament of an everlasting priesthood; because he was zealous for his God, and made entreaty for the sons of Israel. Now let us not think that the testament, or covenant, of life is of this life which we share with beasts and all living things, but of that life which says: I am the life. For indeed our life is hidden with Christ in God, of whom we can say that he himself is also our peace, as the Apostle confirms: For he himself is our peace. God therefore granted to Levi, and through him to his posterity, that they should fear him: For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; and that they should be afraid before his face, or draw back and shrink together, showing the dread of the mind by the shuddering of the body, according to what is written: Upon whom shall I rest, but upon the humble and quiet and him who trembles at my words?
City of God 18.35

A little further on Malachi speaks of Christ, again in the person of God: "My covenant was with him of life and peace, and I gave him fear; and he feared me, and he was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and equity and turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the laws at his mouth because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts." No one should be astonished to hear Christ spoken of as "the angel of the Lord of hosts." He was called his servant because he came to humanity in the form of a servant; similarly he was called an angel because of the evangel, which he brought to humankind.
Commentary on Malachi

The law of truth was in his mouth, that is, the teaching of the apostles, which in a priest ought to be disfigured by no poisoning, but should proceed wholly from the fountain of truth. And iniquity was not found on his lips, so that he may imitate his Lord, of whom it is said: Who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. In peace and in equity he walked with me, so that he may both have peace in himself and make peace for others, and accept no one's person in judgement, and therefore walk with God, as Enoch walked, who was translated to the Lord and was not found: And he turned many away from iniquity. He who is a priest, and does not rebuke those who offend, passes over the office of a priest.
Commentary on Malachi

The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge; he did not say, shall bring forth, but, shall keep, so that they may speak in season, and give their fellow servants their food in due season. And they shall seek the law from his mouth. In Haggai the same is written: Ask the priests the law of the Lord. It belongs to the discipline of a priest, when asked, to answer concerning the law. If, diligent in other matters, he pleads an ignorance that is negligent in the holy Scriptures, he boasts in vain of a dignity whose works he does not display. This is what the apostle Paul writes to Titus: That he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict. And to Timothy: Since from infancy you have known the sacred letters, which can instruct you unto salvation, that you may rebuke sinners before all. There follows: Because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. Ezra, the priest of God, sets forth his own name, that is, Malachi, which is interpreted angel of the Lord; and the priest of God is most truly called an angel, that is, a messenger, because he is the mediator between God and men and announces his will to the peoples; and for this reason the rational is on the breast of the priest, and on the rational doctrine and truth are placed, so that we may learn that a priest ought to be learned, and a herald of the Lord's truth. Some falsely think that what is said to Levi, and through Levi to the priests, is to be understood of Christ, not observing that what follows is contrary to the person of Christ.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

For in sacred language teachers are sometimes called prophets, in that, by pointing out how fleeting are present things, they make manifest the things that are to come. And such the divine discourse convinces of seeing false things, because, while fearing to reprove faults, they vainly flatter evil doers by promising security: neither do they at all discover the iniquity of sinners, since they refrain their voice from chiding. For the language of reproof is the key of discovery, because by chiding it discloses the fault of which even he who has committed it is often himself unaware. Hence Paul says, "That he may be able by sound doctrine even to convince the gainsayers." Hence through Malachi it is said, "The priest's lips keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth." Hence through Isaiah the Lord admonishes, saying, "Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet." For it is true that whosoever enters on the priesthood undertakes the office of a herald, so as to walk, himself crying aloud, before the coming of the judge who follows terribly.
Commentary on Malachi

But you have departed from the way, and have made very many stumble in the law; you have made void the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts. Wherefore I too have made you contemptible and lowly to all peoples, as you have not kept my ways, and have accepted the face in the law. LXX: But you have turned aside from my way, and have made many weak in the law; you have corrupted the testament of Levi, says the Lord Almighty. And I have made you contemptible and dissolute among all the nations, because you have not guarded my ways, but accepted persons in the law. That these things do not pertain to the person of Christ, nor to those who are dedicated to his worship, the prudent reader understands even if I am silent. And the sense is: I wished you to do what is contained in the previous passage, and what I spoke of through Moses in Deuteronomy: Give to Levi his doctrine, and his truth to the just man, and the rest; but you have departed from the right way, or turned aside, though I said: Turn aside neither to the right nor to the left; and you have made many weak in the law, or made them stumble, as Aquila and Symmachus translated. To turn aside to the right is to abstain from foods which God created to be used, to condemn marriage, and to run into what is written in another place: Be not overmuch just. To turn off to the left is when someone gives himself over to luxury and lust, and makes many stumble in the law, someone for whom it is better that an ass's millstone be tied about his neck and he be cast headlong into the sea, than that he should make one of the least stumble. Now those make many weak who, when believers in Christ have received the strength of faith, make them grow weak by the negligence of their own conduct; to them it is most rightly said: You have made void the covenant of Levi, the covenant of life and peace, and the other things which we said pertain to the office of the priest.
Commentary on Malachi

For which reason I too, he says, have made you contemptible and lowly to all peoples, so that they might despise you, and instead of honor and glory trample on you as cast down and lowly: As you have not kept my ways, and have accepted the face in the law. Among all the sins of Levi, or of those who are from Levi, the priests of God, this one is set down as both the last and the greatest: that they accept the face in the law, so that they consider not causes but persons, and, despising the just poor man, receive and honor the unjust rich. To them it is said in Psalm 81 (82): How long do you judge iniquity, and take up the faces of sinners? And Paul to the Galatians: God, he says, does not accept the person of man. And the apostle James rebukes and condemns this sin more fully. But whatever is said to the former people, let us think said to us also, so that we may more cautiously withdraw from vices and not accept the face in the law, nor, we who are worshippers of God, prefer falsehood to truth.
AGAINST HERESIES 4:20.2

Truly, then, the Scripture declared, which says, "First of all believe that there is one God, who has established all things, and completed them, and having caused that from what had no being, all things should come into existence:" He who contains all things, and is Himself contained by no one. Rightly also has Malachi said among the prophets: "Is it not one God who hath established us? Have we not all one Father?" In accordance with this, too, does the apostle say, "There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and in us all." Likewise does the Lord also say: "All things are delivered to Me by My Father;" manifestly by Him who made all things; for He did not deliver to Him the things of another, but His own. But in all things [it is implied that] nothing has been kept back [from Him], and for this reason the same person is the Judge of the living and the dead; "having the key of David: He shall Open, and no man shall shut: He shall shut, and no man shall open." For no one was able, either in heaven or in earth, or under the earth, to open the book of the Father, or to behold Him, with the exception of the Lamb who was slain, and who redeemed us with His own blood, receiving power over all things from the same God who made all things by the Word, and adorned them by [His] Wisdom, when "the Word was made flesh;" that even as the Word of God had the sovereignty in the heavens, so also might He have the sovereignty in earth, inasmuch as [He was] a righteous man, "who did no sin, neither was there found guile in His mouth;" and that He might have the pre-eminence over those things which are under the earth, He Himself being made "the first-begotten of the dead;" and that all things, as I have already said, might behold their King; and that the paternal light might meet with and rest upon the flesh of our Lord, and come to us from His resplendent flesh, and that thus man might attain to immortality, having been invested with the paternal light.
Discourses Against the Arians 2.21.59

But this is God's kindness to humanity, that of whom he is the maker, of them according to grace he afterwards becomes Father also. He becomes, that is, when people, his creatures, receive him into their hearts, as the apostle says, "the spirit of his Son, crying, 'Abba, Father.' " And these are they who, having received the word, gained power from him to become sons of God; for they could not become sons, being by nature creatures, otherwise than by receiving the spirit of the natural and true Son. Wherefore, that this might be, "the word became flesh," that he might make humans capable of godhood. This same meaning may be gained from the prophet Malachi, who says, "Has not one God created us? Have we not all one Father?" For first he puts "created" next to "Father" to show, as the other writers, that from the beginning we were creatures by nature. And God is our Creator through the word, but afterwards we were made sons, and thenceforward God the Creator becomes our Father also.
Commentary on Malachi

Is not one Father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why then does each one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers? Judah has transgressed, and abomination has been done in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has defiled the sanctification of the Lord, which he loved, and has had the daughter of a strange god. May the Lord destroy the man who shall have done this, the master and the disciple, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts. LXX: Is not one Father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why has each one forsaken his brother, so as to make abominable the testament of your fathers? Judah has been forsaken, and abomination has been done in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has defiled the holy things of the Lord, in which he loved, and has devised strange gods. May the Lord destroy the man who does these things, until he is driven out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and from among those who offer sacrifice to the Lord Almighty. Before we discuss the present passage, the tradition of the Hebrews must be set down, or rather the truth of Scripture must be unfolded. We read in the volume that bears the title of Ezra, in the person of Ezra himself speaking: The princes came to me, saying: The people of Israel, and the priests and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands and from their abominations, namely of the Canaanites, and the Hittites and the Perizzites, and the Jebusites, and of the Ammonites, and of the Moabites, and of the Egyptians, and of the Amorites. For they have taken of their daughters for themselves and for their sons, and have mingled the holy seed with the peoples of the lands. The hand also of the princes and magistrates has been first in this transgression. And when I had heard this word, I tore my cloak and my tunic, and plucked out the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down mourning. And again in what follows: And there were found among the sons of the priests those who had married foreign wives: of the sons of Joshua, the son of Jehozadak, and his brothers: Maaseiah, and Eleazar, and Jarib, and Gedaliah; and they gave their hands that they would put away their wives, and offer a ram of the flock for their offence. At the end of the passage also, after the enumeration of those who had taken foreign wives, Scripture records: All these had taken foreign wives, and there were among them women who had borne sons. Having returned, then, from the Babylonian captivity, the princes and the priests and Levites, as well as the rest of the people, cast off their wives of the Israelite race, who, through poverty and the hardship of the long journey, and through the frailty of their sex unable to bear the toil, had been broken down, and had contracted infirmity and unsightliness of body; and they had joined themselves in marriage to foreign women, either in the flower of their age, or more beautiful in the adornment of their bodies, or the daughters of the powerful and rich. So Ezra the prophet rebukes them and calls them to the repudiation of their new spouses, that they may take back the wives whom they had let go: Is not, he says, one father Abraham of us all? Of whom it is written in Isaiah: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah, who bore you, for he was one, and I called him. Has not one God created us, who chose our race out of Abraham? Why then do we despise our old wives, and cast off the daughters of our brothers, so as to forsake the covenant of our fathers and not take wives according to the law?
Commentary on Malachi

Some, not understanding this place, nor knowing the truth of the history, understand what he says, Is not one father of us all?, of Abraham in such a way that they recall that Abraham is the father of the nations too, according to what is written: Is God able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham? Or at any rate they affirm one God the Father, according to what we read in Deuteronomy: Is not this the very Father who possessed you, and made you, and created you? And again: You have forsaken the God who created you. And elsewhere: I have begotten sons and exalted them: but they have forsaken me. And in the volume of the psalms: Strange sons have lied to me, strange sons have grown old and have gone lame from their paths. And those who sinned, departing from this one father, made for themselves many fathers of their vices: For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil. And what follows, Why does each one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers, they have interpreted so as to say: that we all, begotten of one father, ought to be one and to have one lip of confession, but that afterwards, through pride and the building of the tower against God, we were divided into many tongues and opinions. They refer it also to almsgiving, so as to say: that we despise our brothers when we do not share with them what we have received from God for the sustaining of life. And they go on to this, that they assert that according to the Scriptures the Lord is called our brother, he who commanded Mary Magdalene to announce to his brothers that the Lord had risen; and he speaks in the psalm: I will declare your name to my brothers, in the midst of the Church I will sing to you. So the Jews deserted their brother, and defiled the covenant of their fathers, which God had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that in their seed, which is interpreted as Christ, all the nations should be blessed. These things they conjecture in various ways, because they do not find a sure way.
Against Jovinianus 1.10

And if you wish to see more clearly how utterly unlawful it is for a Christian woman to marry a Gentile, consider what the same apostle says, "A wife is bound for so long time as her husband lives. But if the husband be dead, she is freed to be married to whom she will, only in the Lord," that is, to a Christian. The one who allows second and third marriages in the Lord forbids first marriages with a Gentile. Whence Abraham also makes his servant swear upon his thigh, that is, on Christ, who was to spring from his seed, that he would not bring an alien-born as a wife for his son Isaac. And Ezra checked an offense of this kind against God by making his countrymen put away their wives. And the prophet Malachi thus speaks, "Judah has dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah has profaned the holiness of the Lord which he loves and has married the daughter of a strange god. The Lord will cut off the man that does this, him that teaches and him that learns, out of the tents of Jacob, and him that offers an offering to the Lord of hosts." I have said this that they who compare marriage with virginity may at least know that such marriages as these are on a lower level than digamy and trigamy.
Commentary on Malachi

Judah has transgressed; for this tribe returned from Babylon with the priests and Levites; and abomination has been done in Israel and in Jerusalem. Not at all among the ten tribes, which were held by the Assyrians, but among those which returned from Babylon by command of King Cyrus under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah. Because Judah has defiled the sanctification of the Lord, which he loved, and has had the daughter of a strange god, by mingling with foreigners the seed of Israel and of the Gentiles; that is, by taking as wives the daughters of the heathen, who serve idols. Since, therefore, they have done this, the word of the prophet is directed to them, and they are drawn back from sin by curses.
Commentary on Malachi

In short, what follows according to the LXX, Judah has been forsaken, and abomination has been done in Israel, and in Jerusalem, they expound thus: that the Jews have been forsaken because they blasphemed the Lord Savior, and have suffered what is written: According to the multitude of their impieties drive them out, for they have provoked you, O Lord, so that they were scattered as wanderers and fugitives through all the provinces. For they defiled the holy things of the Lord, loving, in place of the Son of God, and devising for themselves, strange gods: For he who does not receive the Son does not receive the Father, who sent him. And therefore, because they did this, they perish for so long, until they are humbled, either by the hardship of captivity or through the consciousness of their sins; and they are cast out of the tabernacles of Jacob, so that, the temple and the altar having been destroyed, sacrificial victims are no longer offered among them. Not content with this explanation — because Judah means confession of the Lord —, they transfer the interpretation to the penitent, who, after he has confessed the Lord, if he sins, does abomination in Israel and in Jerusalem, in the mind that sees God and in the vision of peace. For he pollutes the mysteries of Christ, receiving his body and blood unworthily, because he has loved vices and has devised for himself strange gods, having as many gods as he has sins. According to the apostle Paul: The belly is the god of the gluttonous; and according to James: By whatever one is overcome, to that he is made subject. And he who has done this is driven out of the Church, and out of the tabernacles of Jacob, who supplants vices and sins, until he is humbled for his own good, and a victim is offered for him to the Lord Almighty.
Commentary on Malachi

May the Lord destroy the man who shall have done this. How beautifully he does not cut off pardon from error, nor did he say, May the Lord curse him who has done this, but, who shall have done, stretching the curse into the future, so as to call sinners to repentance. The teacher, he says, and the disciple, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, whether he be a priest or a layman, will be struck by one curse, and there will be no difference of punishment among those in whom the sins are equal. And him who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts: it is understood, may the Lord destroy him also who would wish to offer a gift at the altar for men of this kind, whose only remedy is not to do what they have done.
Commentary on Malachi

What we have expounded specially, according to the book of Ezra, concerning the forsaken wives, others think is said generally against those who plunder what belongs to others and, gathering riches unjustly, dare to offer gifts to God, which he says he can by no means accept, prevented by the tears and weeping and groans of those who have been laid waste; and that this place agrees with that testimony: Honor God from your just labors. But they also insert this sense: that those who, because of the loss of their property, and the death of their children, and shipwreck, and the other things that belong to the loss of worldly goods, are turned to weeping and give themselves wholly to lamentation and groaning, and do not, by strength of mind and hope in God and the rewards of things to come, despise all things, are not received by him even if they direct prayer to God, because they are disfigured by lamentations unbecoming and unfitting for a man.
Commentary on Malachi

And this again you have done: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning, so that I no longer look upon sacrifice, nor accept anything pleasing from your hand. And you have said: For what reason? Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your puberty, whom you have despised; and she is your partner and the wife of your compact. Did not one make, and is the remnant of the spirit his? And what does the one seek, but the seed of God? Guard therefore your spirit; and do not despise the wife of your youth. Since you have hated, put away, says the Lord God of Israel; but iniquity shall cover his garment, says the Lord of hosts. Guard your spirit, and do not despise. LXX: And these things which I hated, you have done: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with lamentation and groaning, from toil still worthy to look upon sacrifice, or to receive anything acceptable from your hands. And you have said: Wherefore? Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have forsaken, and she is your partner, and the wife of your testament, and no other made her, and the remnant of your spirit. And you have said: What else does God seek but seed? And keep guard in your spirit, and do not forsake the wife of your youth; but if, hating her, you put her away, says the Lord God of Israel, impiety shall cover your thoughts, says the Lord Almighty; and keep guard in your spirit, and do not forsake. Let us interpret the history, and, fitting brief statements to the individual verses, let us set out what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews. The Israelite wives, forsaken, and seeing women of foreign nations in their husbands' beds, fled to the help of God alone; prostrate day and night before the altar of the Lord, with tears, groaning and wailing, they cast reproach upon his providence, that it did not look upon human affairs and did not help the wretched. Hence God says that he cannot accept sacrifice and sacrificial victims from the hands of the priests who committed these things, hindered as he is by the weeping and lamentations of the wives; and moreover that they ask for what reason he does not accept sacrifice from their hands; and at once he adds: Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your puberty, whom you have despised, saying: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be in one flesh. And therefore she is called partner, and wife of union and of compact, she who was made by God from the rib of the man.
Commentary on Malachi

Now what follows, Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your puberty, or of your youth, whom you have despised; and she is your partner and the wife of your covenant, or of your testament, ; and no other made her: and the remnant of your spirit, they interpret thus, so as to call the wife of youth the natural understanding and the law written in the heart, which is implanted in all men. Whence also the nations, not having the law of God, do the things that are of the law. Of this spouse, they say, it is proclaimed in Proverbs: A wife is joined to a man by God; and we are commanded to drink from our own waters and fountains, and that no one be partner in the drinking, and that we rejoice with the wife of our youth. This wife impels even the credulous to say: May God judge and may God see; and to him I leave all things between me and you to be judged; of her Ecclesiastes also speaks: And live life with the woman whom you have loved, all the days of your vanity which have been given you under the sun.
AGAINST MARCION 4.34

For in the Gospel of Matthew he says, "Whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery." He also is deemed equally guilty of adultery who marries a woman put away by her husband. The Creator, however, except on account of adultery, does not put asunder that which he himself joined together, the same Moses in another passage enacting that he who had married after violence to a damsel should thenceforth not have it in his power to put away his wife. Now if a compulsory marriage contracted after violence shall be permanent, how much rather shall a voluntary one, the result of an agreement! This has the sanction of the prophet: "You shall not forsake the wife of your youth." Thus you have Christ following spontaneously the tracks of the Creator everywhere, both in permitting divorce and in forbidding it. You find him also protecting marriage, in whatever direction you try to escape. He prohibits divorce when he will have the marriage inviolable; he permits divorce when the marriage is spotted with unfaithfulness. You should blush when you refuse to unite those whom even your Christ has united, and repeat the blush when you disunite them without the good reason why your Christ would have them separated.
Commentary on Malachi

And the remnant of his spirit, whether of God, as some think, or of the husband, as others suppose, because through affection one soul seems in a certain manner to be in two, joined in spirit, united in mind. Since, then, one made both, both the man and the woman, the union of both was therefore made by the Lord, that children might be born. For the one God, what does he seek but the seed of God, that is, sons begotten of the Israelite stock? Since, then, you have fruitful wives and rejoice in children, why do you seek beauty in wives, which is fitting for harlots, not for wives? So God commands through the prophet, and says: Guard your spirit, that you be not led away by lust, that you be not overcome by love of foreign women. And do not despise the wife of your youth, so that she who was first joined to you in virginal marriage may continue until old age.
Commentary on Malachi

This wife is the remnant of our spirit, because she is always joined to our sense; and if she withdraws from us, at once we offend God, and our impiety covers us. Hence again it is urged: Guard your spirit; not the flesh, for those who are in it cannot please God; not the soul: The natural for man does not receive the things that are of the spirit; but the spirit: Because the spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings.
Commentary on Malachi

But it could happen that the princes, priests, Levites and people would answer: God commanded through Moses that when we have hated our wives, we should put them away. And it is to be read: You tell me, it is written: Since you have hated, put away your wife, says the Lord God of Israel. And at once he answered: This was indeed commanded in the law, but because of the hardness of your heart. Which the Lord pursues more fully in the Gospel: But whoever, except for the cause of fornication, unjustly puts away his wife, iniquity shall cover his garment, that is, the body with which the soul is clothed, says the Lord of hosts, so that he may be punished in that very thing in which he sinned. Wherefore, this little question having been resolved, he presses home and repeats what he had said above: Guard your spirit, and do not despise, either the guarding of your spirit, or at any rate your wife, if she is poor or unsightly.
Commentary on Malachi

You have made the Lord labor with your words, and you have said: In what have we made him labor? In this, that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please him; or at any rate, where is the God of judgement? LXX: You who have provoked the Lord with your words, and you have said: In what have we provoked him? In this, that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and in these he is well pleased; and where is the God of justice? This passage is pursued more fully by Psalm 72 (73), whose beginning is: How good is the God of Israel to those who are of right heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well-nigh been poured out. For I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. For there is no regard for their death, and firmness in their stroke. They are not in the labor of men, and with men they will not be scourged. And then: And I said: Then in vain have I justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent. The people, then, having returned from Babylon, and seeing all the nations round about, and those very nations that serve the idols of Babylon, abounding in riches, vigorous in body, possessing in the world all the things that are thought good, while itself, which has the knowledge of God, is covered with squalor, hunger and servitude, is scandalized, and says: There is no providence in human affairs; all things are borne along by uncertain chance and are not governed by the judgement of God; rather, the wicked please him and the good displease him; or at any rate, if God judges all things, where is his equitable and just judgement? A question of this kind the mind that does not believe in things to come raises daily against God; and when it has seen the wicked powerful and the holy humble, the former abounding in all things, the latter not having even what is necessary for sustenance, and sometimes weighed down with deaf ears and blind eyes, and with sores in every part of their limbs, and with infirmity, such as we read of Lazarus in the Gospel, who before the doors of the rich man clothed in purple longed to sustain his needy soul with the crumbs that are thrown away from the leftovers of the tables; but the rich man of such savagery and cruelty that man did not pity man, whom even the tongue of the dogs pitied; not understanding the time of judgement, nor that those are the true goods which are everlasting, they say: The wicked please him, and where is the God of judgement?

Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up. It was such complaints as these that compelled the prophet to anticipate, as it were, the last judgment in which the wicked will be so far from even a pretense of happiness that their misery will be apparent to all, whereas the good, untroubled by even transitory sorrow, will enjoy a manifest and unending blessedness. Malachi had already given a similar illustration of the kind of murmurings that wearied the Lord: "Everyone who does evil is [thought to be] good in the sight of the Lord and as such pleases him." The only point I want to make is that such murmurings against God were the result of an unspiritual interpretation of the law.

And that we may not have to ask, Of what God was the Word made flesh? he does himself previously teach us, saying, "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. The same came as a witness, that he might bear witness of that Light. He was not that Light, but [came] that he might testify of the Light." By what God, then, was John, the forerunner, who testifies of the Light, sent [into the world]? Truly it was by Him, of whom Gabriel is the angel, who also announced the glad tidings of his birth: [that God] who also had promised by the prophets that He would send His messenger before the face of His Son, who should prepare His way, that is, that he should bear witness of that Light in the spirit and power of Elias. But, again, of what God was Elias the servant and the prophet? Of Him who made heaven and earth, as he does himself confess. John, therefore, having been sent by the founder and maker of this world, how could he testify of that Light, which came down from things unspeakable and invisible? For all the heretics have decided that the Demiurge was ignorant of that Power above him, whose witness and herald John is found to be. Wherefore the Lord said that He deemed him "more than a prophet." For all the other prophets preached the advent of the paternal Light, and desired to be worthy of seeing Him whom they preached; but John did both announce [the advent] beforehand, in a like manner as did the others, and actually saw Him when He came, and pointed Him out, and persuaded many to believe on Him, so that he did himself hold the place of both prophet and apostle. For this is to be more than a prophet, because, "first apostles, secondarily prophets;" but all things from one and the same God Himself.

Someone else will appeal to the text, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness," and maintain that whatever is made according to God's image and likeness is man. To support this, numberless instances are adduced to show that in Scripture "man" and "angel" are used indifferently and that the same subject is called both angel and man. This is true of the three who were entertained by Abraham and of the two who came to Sodom. In the whole course of Scripture, persons are styled sometimes men, sometimes angels. Those who hold this view will say that since persons are styled angels who are manifestly men, as when Zechariah says, "The messenger of the Lord, I am with you, says the Lord almighty," and as it is written of John the Baptist, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face," the angels (messengers) of God are so called on account of their nature. Scripture confirms this view that the names applied to higher powers are not those ofspecies of living beings but those of the orders, assigned by God to this and to that reasonable being.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 57: WHY MARK ATTRIBUTES MALACHI'S WORDS TO ISAIAH

WHAT DOES THIS MEAN, THAT ALTHOUGH IT IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET MALACHI, “BEHOLD, I SEND MY ANGEL BEFORE YOUR FACE, WHO WILL PREPARE YOUR WAY BEFORE YOU,” THE EVANGELIST MARK CLAIMS THAT THIS IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET ISAIAH (Mal. 3:1; Mark 1:2)? — Mark could not have been unaware of what he was writing; for he was not lacking in learning, since from childhood he had been immersed in the divine Scriptures and trained in the Law, especially as he had followed the Apostles. Knowing that all sayings must be referred back to their original author, he attributed these words to Isaiah, who had first conveyed this meaning when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3). Accordingly, after the words from Malachi, the Evangelist immediately added, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” so that he might unite the words of both prophets, which relate to one and the same sense, under the name of the earlier prophet.

Of these two comings the prophet Malachi says, "And suddenly there will come to the temple the Lord whom you seek"; that is one coming. Of the second coming he says, " 'And the messenger of the covenant whom you desire, yes, he is coming,' says the Lord of hosts. 'But who will endure the day of his coming? And who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire or like the fuller's lye. He will sit refining and purifying.' " In what immediately follows the Savior himself says, "I will draw near to you for judgment, and I will be swift to bear witness against sorcerers, adulterers and perjurers." It was with this in view that Paul says in due warning: "But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw—the work of each will be made manifest, for the Day of the Lord will declare it, since the day is to be revealed in fire." Paul indicates these two comings also in writing to Titus in these words: "The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men, instructing us, in order that, rejecting ungodliness and worldly lusts, we may live temperately and justly and piously in this world; looking for the blessed hope and glorious coming of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ." Do you see how he speaks of a first coming, for which he gives thanks, and of a second we are going to look for? We find the same lesson in the wording of the creed we profess, as delivered to us, that is, to believe in him who "ascended into heaven and sat down on the right of the Father, and is to come in glory to judge the living and dead, of whose kingdom there will be no end."

And what sort of connexion may this have with what was said before? Much, assuredly, and in full accordance therewith. Yea, by this topic also He proceeds to urge and press them into the faith of Himself; and at the same time likewise, He is speaking in agreement with what had been before said by John. "For if all things are fulfilled even down to John, I am "He that should come." For all the prophets," saith He, "and the law prophesied until John." For the prophets would not have ceased, unless I were come. Expect therefore nothing further, neither wait for any one else. For that I am He is manifest both from the prophets ceasing, and from those that every day "take by force" the faith that is in me. For so manifest is it and certain, that many even take it by force. Why, who hath so taken it? tell me. All who approach it with earnestness of mind.
Then He states also another infallible sign, saying, "If ye will receive it, he is Elias, which was for to come." For "I will send you," it is said, "Elias the Tishbite, who shall turn the heart of the father to the children." This man then is Elias, if ye attend exactly, saith He. For "I will send," saith He, "my messenger before Thy face." And well hath He said, "If ye will receive it," to show the absence of force. For I do not constrain, saith He. And this He said, as requiring a candid mind, and showing that John is Elias, and Elias John. For both of them received one ministry, and both of them became forerunners. Wherefore neither did He simply say, "This is Elias," but, "If ye are willing to receive it, this is he," that is, if with a candid mind ye give heed to what is going on. And He did not stop even at this, but to the words, "This is Elias, which was for to come," He added, to show that understanding is needed, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."
Commentary on Malachi

Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and at once the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the testament whom you desire. LXX: Behold, I will send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of justice whom you desire. The Lord in the Gospel interpreted this of John the Baptist, saying: This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I will send my angel before your face, and he will prepare your way before me; nor did he use the same words which the LXX translators rendered. Mark the evangelist also, weaving together two testimonies, of Malachi and of Isaiah, under the utterance of one prophet, began thus: The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way. This, though in other words, we read in Malachi. But what follows, The voice of one crying in the desert, prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight, is said by Isaiah the prophet; and at once, explaining of whom both testimonies are said: There was, he says, John in the desert, baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins. But the evangelists too interpreted the prophecy of the prophets concerning John, and while they agree in sense, they differ in words. For whereas the LXX rendered: Make the paths of our God straight, Mark and Luke said: Make his paths straight. But John: Make straight, he says, the way of the Lord. From which it is clear that the apostles and evangelists, and the Lord Savior himself, do not follow the authority of the LXX translators, which, having knowledge of the Hebrew tongue, they do not need, but translate from the Hebrew what they had read, not caring about the syllables and points of the words, provided that the truth of the sense is carried over. That they did this in many places we have indeed shown, and especially in that book which we entitled 'On the Best Kind of Translating' it has been proved by many testimonies together. This, then, which is said, Behold, I send my angel and he will prepare the way before my face, is said in the person of Christ, because he sent John into the desert of Judea to preach the baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins. But what follows, And at once the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the testament whom you desire, he thus speaks of himself as of another, according to the custom of the Scriptures. And no one doubts that this Ruler is the Savior, who is the Creator of all things, and is called the angel of the testament and the angel of great counsel. Others, however, think that what is said, Behold, I send my angel and he will prepare the way before my face, is said in the person of the Father; and what follows, At once the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the testament whom you desire, they understand to have been said by him of the Lord Savior. Now John prepares the way and makes the paths of our God straight in the hearts of believers, in which, because of depravity and unbelief, God could not walk before. And the temple they interpret either as the Church or as each one of the believers in the Church: Be built up as spiritual houses, a holy priesthood; to offer spiritual victims, and acceptable to God through Christ Jesus. And those who have believed: Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you? The Jews understand what is said, Behold, I send my angel, as said of Elijah the prophet, and what follows, At once the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the testament whom you desire, they refer to the ἠλειμμένον, that is, their Christ, who they say will come in the last time. But I wonder how the outcome of events does not teach them the truth. For what temple of his will the Ruler find, when it has been destroyed to its foundations? Or if it is to be built by another before Christ comes, what more will their Christ do, when all things have been restored by another? Our Lord in the Gospel, interpreting Elijah the prophet as John the Baptist, says: If you wish to know, he is Elijah who is to come, of whom also this same prophet whom we are now discussing writes at the end: Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And how John is Elijah, he has given us the way of understanding, recalling that he came in the power and spirit of Elijah.
Commentary on Malachi

For he enters like the fire of a smelter and like the herb of the washers; and he will sit refining and cleansing as silver, and as gold; and he will cleanse the sons of Levi, and will pour them out like gold and like silver, and they will be offering sacrificial victims to the Lord in justice; and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as in the former days, and as in the earlier years. And I will draw near to you in judgement, and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against those who swear falsely by my name. And those who defraud hirelings of their wages, and oppress widows by their power, and strike orphans, and pervert the judgement of the sojourner, and who do not fear me, says the Lord Almighty, for I am the Lord your God, and I do not change. Above we read of a question raised against the Lord by those who say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please him; or at any rate, if they displease him, where is the God of judgement? That is, where is the truth of justice? To resolve it the word of the Lord answered: I will send my angel, who will prepare my way, and the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, he who is the judge of truth, of whom it is said in the psalm: O God, give your judgement to the king, and your justice to the king's son. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son. And he is the angel of the testament whom you seek, whom evil things do not please, who does not accept persons in judgement, who is changed by no mercy and no severity: For in the hand of the Lord there is a cup of pure wine, full of mixture, and he has poured it from this into this, that is, mercy tempers justice, and justice mercy. This one, therefore, will come at once and swiftly to his temple, that is, the Church.

For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. He was preparing the souls of believers, in which the Lord was going to walk, so that he, the pure one, might walk in most pure ways, saying: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Porphyry compares this passage with the beginning of the evangelist Mark, in which it is written: The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way; the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. For since the testimony is woven together from Malachi and Isaiah, he asks how we can think the example was taken as from Isaiah alone. To him churchmen have answered most fully. We, however, think either that the name of Isaiah was added through the fault of copyists, which we can prove in other places as well, or at any rate that one body has been made out of different testimonies of the Scriptures. And because to the prophetic privilege there was added also the Baptist's reward, that he should baptize his own Lord, he therefore brings in an αὔξησιν (increase) of his merits, producing the testimony from Malachi in which he is even proclaimed an angel. Speaking further of Christ in the same vein, Malachi says, "Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And presently the Lord, whom you seek, and the angel of the testament whom you desire, shall come into the temple. Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts. And who shall be able to think of the day of his coming? And who shall stand to see him?" In this text he foretells both comings of Christ, the first and the second—the first where he says, "And presently the Lord shall come into his temple." Since then it is evident that many are to judge with the Lord but that others are to be judged, not however on equality but according to their deserts, he will come with all his angels. [At the judgment] before him shall be gathered all nations, and among all the angels are to be reckoned those that have been so perfect, that sitting upon twelve thrones they judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Of John the Baptist it is said, "Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you."
AGAINST CELSUS 4:13

But as it is in mockery that Celsus says we speak of "God coming down like a torturer bearing fire" and thus compels us unseasonably to investigate words of deeper meaning, we shall make a few remarks, sufficient to enable our hearers to form an idea of the defense which disposes of the ridicule of Celsus against us. And then we shall turn to what follows. The divine word says that our God is "a consuming fire" and that "he draws rivers of fire before him." He even enters in as "a refiner's fire and as a fuller's herb," to purify his own people. But when he is said to be a "consuming fire," we inquire what are the things that are appropriate to be consumed by God. And we assert that it is wickedness, and the works which result from it, which are being figuratively called "wood, hay, stubble," God consumes as a fire.
Commentary on Malachi

And who will be able to think of the day of his coming? If no one can think of it, because of the power of his majesty, who will be able to bear it? And who will stand to see him, that is, who will be able with bleary and half-blind eyes to look upon him in his brightness, who is the Sun of justice, and in whose wings is healing? He will come like a refining fire, and like fullers' herb. Fire for shall burn before him, and round about him a mighty tempest. Then he will call the heaven from above, and the earth, that he may judge his people; rivers of fire will flow before him, rolling along every sinner. Now the Lord is called fire, and a consuming fire, that he may burn up our wood, hay and stubble. And not only fire, but also fullers' herb, which in Hebrew is called borith, and the LXX render πόαν, that is, fullers' herb. To those who sin gravely he is a refining and consuming fire; but to those who commit light sins, fullers' herb, so as to restore cleanness to those who have been washed, according to what is written in Isaiah: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgement and by the spirit of burning. Those who have filth need the spirit of judgement, that they may be washed; those who are full of blood need the spirit of burning, that the blood which has been smeared on them from without may be taken away.
Commentary on Malachi

And he will sit refining and cleansing as silver, so that, according to Ezekiel, whatever bronze, tin, iron and lead has been mixed into our gold and silver, that is, into our sense and our speech, may be thoroughly smelted in the furnace of the Lord, so that pure gold and silver may remain. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn, and he will purify the sons of Levi. For it is time that judgement begin from the house of God. And elsewhere it is written: Begin from my holy ones. In the sons of Levi, understand the whole priestly dignity. But if the priests must be purified and strained, so that pure gold and silver may remain, what is to be said of the rest?
Commentary on Malachi

When they have been cleansed and strained, then they will offer just sacrifices to the Lord, and their sacrifice will please, which they offer for Judah and Jerusalem, that is, for those who confess the Lord and behold his peace with the mind, as the days of the age, and as the ancient years, so that as in the beginning they pleased God, so after sin and repentance they may begin to please, when they have been purged of every filth of sins.
Commentary on Malachi

And I will draw near, he says, to you in judgement, and I will be a swift witness. How great is the dread of the judgement, since he himself is both witness and judge. And he is a witness against all sorcerers and adulterers, for these crimes are committed in secret, and therefore they are brought out into the open, lest they lie hidden long. After the sorcerers are placed the adulterers, after the adulterers the perjurers, after the perjurers those who wrong the hireling over his wages and will not pay what they owe for the labor of the work. Widows also and orphans they wrong, as is understood; and they oppress the stranger and the foreigner, or at any rate the catechumen, who has not yet been made a citizen in the city of Christ. And even if they have not done all these things, the one crime that they have not feared the Lord suffices for their punishment. Let us therefore by no means think them light sins, perjury, and not paying the laborer his wages, and wronging the widow and the orphan, and oppressing the foreigner and the stranger, which are compared to sorcery, and poisonings, and adultery. These things we understand according to the history and according to tropology, so that what was said at that time to the leaders of the Jews is now said to the leaders of the churches.
AGAINST CELSUS 4:14

But let us look at what Celsus next with ostentation announces in the following fashion: "And again," he says, "let us resume the subject from the beginning, with a larger array of proofs. And I make no new proofs. And I make no new statement but say what has long been settled. God is good and beautiful and blessed, and that in the best and most beautiful degree. But if he comes down among humanity, he must undergo a change, and a change from good to evil, from virtue to vice, from happiness to misery, and from best to worst. Who, then, would make a choice of such a change? It is the nature of a mortal, indeed, to undergo change and remolding, but of an immortal to remain the same and unaltered. God, then, could not admit such a change." Now it appears to me that the fitting answer has been returned to these objections when I have related what I called in Scripture the "condescension" of God to human affairs. For [this] purpose he did not need to undergo a transformation, as Celsus thinks we assert, nor a change from good to evil, nor from virtue to vice, nor from happiness to misery, nor from best to worst. For, continuing unchangeable in his essence, he condescends to human affairs by the economy of his providence. We show accordingly that the holy Scripture represents God as unchangeable, both by such words as "you are the same" and "I change not." Whereas the gods of Epicurus, being composed of atoms, and, so far as their structure is concerned, capable of dissolution, endeavor to throw off the atoms which contain the elements of destruction. Even the god of the Stoics, as being corporeal, at one time has his whole essence composed of the guiding principle when the conflagration [of the world] takes place; and at another, when a rearrangement of things occurs, he again becomes partly material. For even the Stoics were unable to comprehend distinctly the natural idea of God as a being altogether incorruptible and simple and uncompounded and indivisible.
ON THE TRINITY 11:47

He does not lack things that are of Him and through Him and in Him. The Source and Maker of all, Who contains all, Who is beyond all, does not need that which is within Him, the Creator His creatures, the Possessor His possessions. Nothing is prior to Him, nothing derived from any other than Him, nothing beyond Him. What element of fulness is still lacking in God, which time will supply to make Him all in all? Whence can He receive it, if outside Him is nothing, and while nothing is outside Him, He is eternally Himself? And if He is eternally Himself, and there is nothing outside Him, with what increase shall He be made full, by what addition shall He be made other than He is? Did He not say, I am and I change not? What possibility is there of change in Him? What scope for progress? What is prior to eternity? What more divine than God? The subjection of the Son will not therefore make God to be all in all, nor will any cause perfect Him, from Whom and through Whom and in Whom are all causes. He remains God as He ever was, and He needs nothing further, for what He is, He is eternally of Himself and for Himself.
Commentary on Malachi

And what follows, I am the Lord and I do not change, he sets down for this reason, because he had said above, He is like a refining fire, and like fullers' herb, lest we should think that he changes the nature of his divinity when for our sake he is named either angel, or fire, or borith.
Commentary on Malachi

And you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed.

For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my ordinances, and have not kept them. LXX: And you, sons of Jacob, have not departed from the sins of your fathers; you have turned aside from my ordinances, and have not kept them. He had said above: I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers and the adulterers and the perjurers, and those who wrong the hireling over his wages, the widows and the orphans, and oppress the stranger and have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts. And saying that he is a just judge, in that he does not accept persons in judgement, he added: I am the Lord, and I do not change. And the sense is: You change every day through sorceries and adulteries and perjuries and false accusations and violence; I in judgement am changed by no difference of persons. And though I confess that I am a severe and just judge, O sons of Jacob, yet you have not been consumed by the variety of torments, according to that which is written in Jeremiah: In vain have I struck your sons; you have not received discipline; nor do you do this lately, nor once, so that you might deserve pardon for error, but you hold an inherited impiety, departing from my ordinances from the days of your fathers, and not keeping what I commanded. But the sons of Jacob according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), sons of the supplanter who snatched his brother's birthright, who do not depart from the sins of their fathers, and turn aside from the ordinances, and do not keep what has been commanded, let us understand as those who, though placed in the Church, do not depart from vices, and take to themselves the false name of the Christian religion.

And while God is provoked with frequent and continual offenses, he softens his indignation, and in his patience waits for the day of retribution, once for all determined. And although he has revenge in his power, he prefers to keep patience for a long while. [He bears], that is to say, mercifully, and puts off, so that, if it might be possible, the long-protracted mischief may at some time be changed, and humanity, involved in the contagion of errors and crimes, may even though late be converted to God, as he himself warns and says, "I do not will the death of him that dies, so much as that he may return and live." And again, " 'Return unto me,' says the Lord."
Commentary on Malachi

We have heard the history of Ezra; now let us take up again the words of the prophet, looking more carefully whether prophecy and history agree. When it is said: Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord Almighty, it is clear that those whom he exhorts to come back had departed from the Lord. And see the mercy of the Lord: he promises like for like, that with the measure they have measured, it may be measured back to them. And just as it is written in Leviticus: If you walk perversely towards me, I too will walk against you with perverse fury, so now too he exhorts the people to return, so that he himself also may return to them. They, not understanding that they have departed from the Lord, shamelessly ask: In what shall we return? And they say: For when did we depart, that we should rightly be compelled to come back?
Commentary on Malachi

We can also interpret the tithes and first fruits thus: If someone learned and instructed in the law of God is able to instruct others, he ought not to attribute it to his own prudence and to the talent that he possesses; but let him give thanks first to God, who bestows all things, then to his priests and teachers, by whom he was taught. For if he does not give thanks, but claims knowledge for himself, he will be cursed in want. But if, understanding God to be the giver, and giving thanks to those through whom he was instructed by God, he humbles himself and brings food into the storehouse of God, that is, ministers the nourishment of holy Scripture to the peoples in the Church, at once the floodgates of heaven will be opened over him, and spiritual rain will be poured out; and God will command his clouds to rain a shower upon him, and he will enjoy abundance of all things; and he will also rebuke for his sake the devourer, that is, the opposing powers, and his labour will bring forth fruit, and he will attain that which is written: Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear. He will also lift up his eyes and see the regions, that they are already white for the harvest; and he will gather fruits unto eternal life. Nor will the vine be barren in his field, he who says in the Gospel: I am the vine. And he who speaks through the prophet: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true; and such — through the confession of humility, and the giving of thanks to God and to the teachers of his Church — blessedness will he attain that all nations will call him blessed, and those who have heard him discoursing in the Church will long to dwell in his land and his teaching.
Commentary on Malachi

Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts. And you have said: In what shall we return?

Will a man fix God, since you fix me? And you have said: In what have we fixed you? In tithes and in first fruits. In want you are cursed, and you have fixed me, the whole nation. Bring every tithe into the storehouse, and let there be food in my house, and prove me in this, says the Lord: if I do not open to you the floodgates of heaven, and pour out on you a blessing even to abundance. And I will rebuke for your sake the devourer, and he will not spoil the fruit of your vine, nor will the vine in the field be barren, says the Lord of hosts. And all the nations will call you blessed; for you will be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord Almighty. And you have said: In what shall we return? Does a man supplant God, since you have supplanted me? And you have said: In what have we supplanted you? Because the tithes and the first fruits are with you, and you, seeing, look on, and you supplant me. The year is completed, and you have brought the fruits into your treasuries, and there will be plunder in your houses. Return, therefore, in this, says the Lord Almighty. If I do not open to you the floodgates of heaven, and pour out on you my blessing until it suffices, and I will deal out food to you, and I will not destroy the fruit of your land, and your vine in the field will not be weakened, says the Lord Almighty; and all the nations will call you blessed, because you will be as a willing land, says the Lord Almighty. We also said at the beginning that by the prophet Malachi Ezra the priest ought to be understood, and that all the things that are written in his history are contained in this volume too; and now we say that in the times of him and of Nehemiah — who clearly lived at the same time — there was a most grievous famine, and because of the famine an uprising, and that the poor, compelled by the necessity of their circumstances, sold their sons and daughters, and every possession, and their whole substance. In short, they say: Our sons and our daughters are very many; let us take grain as their price, and let us eat and live. And there were those who said: Let us pledge our fields and vineyards and our houses, and let us take grain in the famine. And I was very angry, says Ezra, when I had heard their outcry according to these words, and my heart took counsel with me, and I rebuked the nobles and the magistrates, and the rest. So in the time of famine the price of grain was very dear, so much so that they were compelled to sell their own sons; and both those who had little and those who had gathered much produce into their storehouses, by necessity or by the greatness of the price, were unwilling to render the tithes to the Levites, who had no share in the inheritance of Judea, but the first fruits and the tithes were their inheritance. And lest this be thought to be our own, let us set down the testimony of Ezra: And I learned, he says, that the portions of the Levites had not been given, and each one of the Levites, and of the singers, and of those who ministered, had fled to his own country. And I pleaded the case against the magistrates, and said: Why do we forsake the house of God? And I gathered them together, and made them stand in their stations. And all Judah brought the tithes of grain, wine and oil into the storehouses. And we set over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest and Zadok the scribe, and so on.

The Lord answered: Will a man fix God, since you fix me? The Hebrew word that is written haiecba the LXX translated 'if he supplants', in place of which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put 'if he defrauds', so that the sense is: Does a man defraud God, since you defraud me? And indeed, according to the order of the history, because the people were not rendering the tithes and the first fruits to the Levites, the Lord says that he himself suffers fraud, since his ministers, compelled by famine and want, had deserted the temple. For if it is he who is visited in prison through others, and taken in when sick, and receives food and is given drink when hungry and thirsty, why should he himself not receive tithes in his ministers; and, if they are not given, himself be deprived of his share? This haiecba of which we have spoken is translated in the language of the Syrians and Chaldeans as 'if he will fix'; whence we too translated it so many years ago, referring it more to the mystery of the Lord's passion, in which men crucified God, than to the tithes and first fruits that are written of. Let the prudent reader ask how our translation agrees with what follows: In tithes and in first fruits, and let him see whether we can say this: That you might fix me to the cross, that you might lay wicked hands on your God, you brought about by the premeditation of many things beforehand, by withholding the tithes and first fruits, I do not say from my priests and Levites, but from me, who commanded through Moses that they be given. Let this be said by us about a single word, as we leave the judgement of its interpretation to the reader's discretion; now let us follow the order of the prophecy.
Commentary on Malachi

What we have said of the tithes and first fruits, which were once given by the people to the priests and Levites, understand also of the peoples of the Church, who have been commanded not only to give tithes and first fruits, but also to sell all that they have and give to the poor and follow the Lord and Savior. But if we are unwilling to do this, let us at least imitate the beginnings of the Jews, so that we give to the poor a part of the whole, and pay due honour to the priests and Levites. Hence the Apostle too says: Honour widows who are widows indeed; and that the presbyter is to be honoured with double honour, especially he who labours in the word and in the teaching of God. Whoever does not do this is convicted of defrauding and supplanting God, and he is cursed in the want of all things, so that he who has sown sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who has sown in blessing will gather fruits abundantly in blessings. If ever famine and want and the lack of all things oppress the world, let us know that this comes down from the wrath of God, who says that he is defrauded in the poor, if they do not receive alms, and is deprived of his own possession.
Commentary on Malachi

Because you have not rendered to me the tithes and first fruits, therefore you are cursed in famine and want, and you supplant me, or defraud and deprive me, the whole nation. For 'nation', which in the Hebrew is written aggoi, the Seventy translated 'year', ἔτος instead of ἔθνος. And the sense is: Behold, the year is completed, and you have carried nothing into my treasuries, but everything into your own storehouses. And for the sake of tithes and first fruits, which were small things if they had been given by you, you have lost the richness of your possessions and all abundance of produce.
Commentary on Malachi

But so that you may know that this was brought about by my anger, because you defrauded me of my share, I exhort you and admonish you to bring the tithes into the storehouses, that is, into the treasuries of the temple, and let the priests and Levites who minister to me have food; and prove me, whether I do not pour out such great rains that the floodgates of heaven will be believed to have been opened. And I will pour out on you a blessing even to abundance. The word 'pouring out' shows the name of bounty.

But it can happen that, with rains watering the fields, there is indeed fertility; but either the locust comes, or the cankerworm, or blight, or the caterpillar, and the labours of men perish; therefore he joins to it and says: And I will rebuke for your sake the devourer, the locust, that is, and the rest that we have mentioned: And he will not spoil the fruit of your land. The vine also will fill the winepresses, and all the nations round about will marvel at the fertility of your land, so much so that all will long to dwell in it, and you will be an example to all nations of abundance in all things.
